clue.text: Element suggesting singular state to Latinist and leader (or first in book) to Muslim

definitions.text: Element suggesting singular state to Latinist

parts.note: a caliph, also spelt calif, is a Muslim ruler and leader, which the words 'to Muslim' confirm
taken as written

indicators.note: 'first in book' says the first item is placed inside the word for a book

parts.note: Num. is the abbreviation for Numbers, a book of the Old Testament
I is the Roman numeral one, so the first

explanation.surface: A puzzling chemistry riddle about an element's name sounding Latin and having a Muslim ruler at its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to Muslim' only says whose leader is meant. The definition plays on Latin: if the state's name were a neuter plural, its singular would end in -um, as this element's name does.
explanation.definitionFit: Californium is a radioactive chemical element named after the US state of California, whose name looks like a Latin plural.

clue.text: Oo!

parts.note: the clue itself is two round characters, an exclamation of surprise that is also a pair of ring-shaped letters of the alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a picture: the two O's are letters that are circles, and the exclamation 'Oo!' is just the cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Two O characters are literally letters shaped like circles, and the phrase also names mass-mailed notices.

clue.text: Smallest article's broken in case

indicators.note: the article is said to be broken into the next phrase, so it sits inside that word

parts.note: lest means for fear that, in case
A is the indefinite article; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A small item is described as smashed inside its protective box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken in' looks like damage, but it puts A inside LEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Least is the superlative of little, so it means smallest in amount or size.

clue.text: Sweet and loving social worker

parts.note: fond means affectionate, loving
an ant is a social insect, and worker ants are the labourers of the colony

explanation.surface: A kind, affectionate social worker is praised as a sweet person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' suggests a job in welfare services; here it is the insect that lives in a colony.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondant is a soft creamy confection, a sweet in British usage for a piece of candy.

clue.text: Have house outside university to get rest

indicators.note: the dwelling word goes outside the abbreviation for university, wrapping round it

parts.note: to reside is to have one's house or home somewhere

explanation.surface: Someone lives off campus in order to get some rest from student life.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is what is left over, the rest or remainder.

clue.text: Spectral shower makes one get up (including policeman)

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word for getting up is said to include the policeman, so he goes inside it

parts.note: to rise is to get up out of bed
a cop is an informal word for a policeman

explanation.surface: A ghostly figure frightens someone into getting out of bed, with a constable present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectral shower' suggests a ghost appearing; it means an instrument showing the spectrum. 'get up' could be a disguise or costume but is the verb RISE.
explanation.definitionFit: An iriscope is a device that displays the colours of the spectrum, so it shows spectra.

clue.text: Death during dinner at operational centre awaiting reopening for 26 (with the 13 and the 14)

definitions.text: awaiting reopening for 26 (with the 13 and the 14)

indicators.note: the death word occurs during the meal, so it is placed inside it

parts.note: a meal such as dinner
mori is Latin for to die, familiar from memento mori, a reminder of death
an operating theatre is the centre of surgical operations in a hospital

explanation.surface: Someone dies at a hospital dinner near the operating theatre, which awaits reopening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'operational centre' is the operating theatre of a hospital. The definition refers to the Stratford venues of Shakespeare (26): this one, the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, was being rebuilt in 2010, as was the Swan (13), while The Other Place (14) had also closed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare Memorial Theatre is the old name of the main Stratford playhouse, closed for rebuilding when this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Counter to sound of group swear word?

indicators.note: the clue asks for what the group's name plus a swear word sound like when spoken

parts.note: Abba is a famous Swedish pop group; a cuss is a swear word, an oath

explanation.surface: A question about whether a pop band's name plus a curse could be a counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' looks like a person who counts or a shop surface; it is the bead frame for counting.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame with sliding beads used for counting, so a counter.

clue.text: Summons man to squirm

parts.note: a writ is a legal document such as a summons
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A court summons arrives and makes a man squirm.
explanation.definitionFit: To writhe is to twist and contort the body, as in pain or discomfort, so squirm.

clue.text: Return 16 down is cheap at the price

parts.note: the answer to 16 down means barred, read here as given a bar placed before it
a gain is a return or profit on an investment

explanation.surface: A profit described as banned turns out to be good value.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 down is BARRED, and the return is read as 'barred', that is, fitted with BAR in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain is something bought for less than its worth, so cheap at the price.

clue.text: Shed fitful light on man in Southsea (in France)

indicators.note: the man is placed inside the letters for south and the French sea

parts.note: S is south and mer is French for sea; Southsea is a seaside district of Portsmouth on the English south coast
him is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: Someone casts flickering light on a man standing in the seaside resort of Southsea, oddly transported to France.
explanation.walkthrough: Southsea is a resort in Portsmouth, England, but here it splits into SOUTH and SEA, with SEA put into French.
explanation.definitionFit: To shimmer is to shine with a wavering, flickering light, so shed fitful light.

clue.text: Make love by measure in place of 6 (and the 13 and the 14)

parts.note: to court is to woo, the old sense of making love
a yard is a unit of measure of length

explanation.surface: A romance blossoms in the yard where the theatres used to stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make love' is the old sense of wooing. The Courtyard Theatre in Stratford was the temporary home of the Royal Shakespeare Company while the main theatre (6), the Swan (13) and The Other Place (14) were out of use.
explanation.definitionFit: The Courtyard Theatre stood in for the Stratford playhouses during their rebuilding, so it took their place.

clue.text: Sound of red plant applied to gold

indicators.note: the clue says the root vegetable is spoken, giving a word said the same way

parts.note: a carrot is a plant with an orange-red root, the colour of red hair called carroty

explanation.surface: A red-leaved plant is gilded, as if for a garden ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: Carrot-coloured, or carroty, is a way to describe red hair, so the red plant is the carrot.
explanation.definitionFit: The carat is the measure of purity applied to gold, as in 24-carat gold.

clue.text: Pole with pale on river

parts.note: S is the south pole, one of the compass points
wan means pale, sickly

explanation.surface: A Pole with a pallid face stands by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a nationality; it is a magnetic pole, south. The Swan is a river in Western Australia, and the Swan is also a Stratford theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swan River flows through Perth in Western Australia, named after its black swans.

clue.text: In old English, revision of chapter left by Lords to Commons

indicators.note: the old English abbreviation goes round the rest, which sits in it
a revision reworks text, so the letters of chapter and left are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bill about Old English is revised and sent from the House of Lords to the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament each House refers to the other obliquely as 'the other place'; it is also the name of a Stratford theatre. 'chapter' looks like part of a bill but is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: By parliamentary convention, members of each chamber refer to the other House obliquely by this phrase.

clue.text: My old man (if grand) with a tax cruelly inflicted on rabbits

indicators.note: cruelly suggests violent treatment, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: the Grand Old Man was the nickname of the British prime minister Gladstone, abbreviated GOM; without the grand, old man is OM

explanation.surface: A grandfather complains about a tax as cruel as anything done to rabbits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cruelly' rearranges OM, A and TAX into XOMATA. Myxomata are the tumours of myxomatosis, the viral disease deliberately spread to control rabbits.
explanation.definitionFit: Myxomata are the jelly-like tumours caused by myxomatosis, a disease deliberately spread among rabbit populations.

clue.text: Phone call by layabout ("I'm disgusted") evokes profound amusement

parts.note: to give someone a bell is British slang for a phone call
read as two words, lay plus about, the three letters of lay scrambled
ugh is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A lazy caller's disgusted remark on the phone makes someone laugh out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'layabout' is read as LAY + 'about', an anagram of LAY giving YLA. Giving someone 'a bell' is British slang for phoning them.
explanation.definitionFit: A belly laugh is a deep hearty laugh, an expression of deep amusement.

clue.text: 26 said to be blackballed?

indicators.note: said means spoken aloud, the poet's title sounding like another word

parts.note: Shakespeare, the answer to 26 across, is known as the Bard

explanation.surface: Is the great playwright reported as excluded from a club?
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare is traditionally called the Bard (of Avon).
explanation.definitionFit: To be blackballed is to be voted out of a club, effectively barred from membership.

clue.text: I'm on my way out after a small amount of torpor

indicators.note: the dying words come after the small amount in the answer

parts.note: cc, cubic centimetre, is a small amount of liquid
I die is what someone on the way out, dying, might say

explanation.surface: Someone feels they are dying after a small dose of lethargy.
explanation.walkthrough: Accidie is an old word, used by Chaucer, for spiritual sloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Accidie is sloth or apathy, traditionally the sin of spiritual laziness, so a state of torpor.

clue.text: Go quietly to hide bereavement in Derbyshire

indicators.note: the go and quiet letters hide the loss within them

parts.note: taken as written
a bereavement is a loss of a loved one
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Advice to grieve quietly and keep your loss hidden, set in Derbyshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Glossop is a town in Derbyshire, a county in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossop is a market town in the High Peak district of Derbyshire, so it is located there.

clue.text: Attempt at crazy return

indicators.note: return means the crazy word comes back, read backwards

parts.note: bats is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: An attempt at a mad comeback.
explanation.definitionFit: A stab is an informal word for a try or attempt, as in have a stab at it.

clue.text: Poet's name used by his first lady

parts.note: his refers to the poet, Shelley, whose first letter is S
she is the pronoun for a lady

explanation.surface: A poet's name is used by his first wife.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Percy Bysshe Shelley; 'his first' is the first letter of Shelley, not of 'his'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bysshe is the middle name of the Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley.

clue.text: Philosopher in 26 losing house to relation

indicators.note: losing means the house is taken away from the philosopher's name

parts.note: Horatio in Hamlet is told there are more things in heaven and earth than dreamt of in his philosophy

explanation.surface: A philosophical character from Shakespeare loses his home to a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet tells Horatio, 'There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio is a quantitative relation between two amounts, such as three to one.

clue.text: Go over to the piano in St Peter's pub in Gwent

parts.note: to cross is to go over, as a road
a piano is played on its keys

explanation.surface: Someone walks over to the piano in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: St Peter holds the keys of heaven, so crossed keys are his emblem and a common pub name; Crosskeys is also a town in Gwent, a Welsh county.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossed keys are the emblem of St Peter and a pub sign, and Crosskeys is a town in Gwent.

clue.text: Some Pan-pipes for a country

indicators.note: some of the pipes word is taken, its last letters dropped

parts.note: a syrinx is a set of panpipes, named after the nymph Syrinx pursued by the god Pan

explanation.surface: Part of a set of pipes is traded for a whole country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' cuts the last two letters NX from SYRINX. Syrinx was the nymph who became reeds that Pan made into pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a country in the Middle East.

clue.text: Topless announcer keeps setter green

indicators.note: the announcer keeps the setter inside, holding it within
topless means the announcer word loses its top, first letter

parts.note: a herald is an announcer of news
me is the crossword setter referring to themself

explanation.surface: A bare-chested announcer holds on to a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' removes H from HERALD, leaving ERALD, which keeps ME. 'green' looks like inexperienced, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Emerald is a bright green colour, named after the gemstone.

clue.text: Extent of time to time the Royal 26 Company's refurbishment?

indicators.note: refurbishing remodels a building, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: RSC, the Royal Shakespeare Company, with 26 standing for Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A question about how long the Royal Shakespeare Company's building works will take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refurbishment' rearranges T, THE and RSC; the RSC was then refurbishing its Stratford theatres.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch is a continuous period, an extent of time, as in a two-year stretch.

clue.text: Spooner has uttered: "Utter poet!"

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the starts of words, so his version is wanted

parts.note: spake is the old past tense of speak, meaning uttered
utter as an adjective means sheer, complete

explanation.surface: An exclamation, credited to Spooner, condemning a poet as utterly bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like a verb but is the adjective SHEER; SPAKE SHEER with its opening sounds swapped becomes the poet's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare is the most famous English poet and playwright.
